title: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
description: An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.Eyewitnesses share
body: An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery. On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges. It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

schema.headline: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion

title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling
description: Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has
body: Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report."Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick. While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders.Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

schema.headline: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling

title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
description: Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.The pair were technicians working
body: Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war. The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.Italy's foreign minister was quoted by Italian media as saying that investigations showed that the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran and that Iranian proxies were known to carry out attacks in the region."The Rheinmetall Group is in deep mourning," the German firm said in a statement confirming the deaths of two of its staff members."Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, as they were providing technical support for air defence systems," it added."Protecting people in the country was a matter of profound importance to them."Company management and the workforce are devastated that our colleagues have now lost their lives."Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.The men had been performing maintenance on systems used by the Kuwait Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa citing Italy's foreign ministry.Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families. "My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf."Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

schema.headline: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility

title: Rebecca Taylor: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
description: A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a pr
body: A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning. The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update. The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said."It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying. All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed. The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

schema.headline: Rebecca Taylor: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment

title: New Zealand: Ruling coalition loses parliamentary majority
description: New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillu
body: New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table."There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc. But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership."There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.

schema.headline: New Zealand: Ruling coalition loses parliamentary majority

title: Guinea orders mass clean-up in Conakry months after deadly rubbish dump collapse
description: Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.Prime
body: Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday announced a deadline of 31 December  to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.He said much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs."The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said."Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a new disposal site in Baretodé, outside the capital.The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

schema.headline: Guinea orders mass clean-up in Conakry months after deadly rubbish dump collapse

title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
description: The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.The treaties were published on Thur
body: The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released. Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements.""It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning. However, the UK will not be given voting rights.Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny. Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

schema.headline: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause

title: Lenacapavir: Uganda and Zambia lead rollout of low-cost HIV prevention jab
description: Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to t
body: Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025.The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection."These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday. More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

schema.headline: Lenacapavir: Uganda and Zambia lead rollout of low-cost HIV prevention jab

title: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza
description: A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.Local sour
body: A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month."No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

schema.headline: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza

title: Indonesia: 13 dead in mine disaster that highlights illegal hunt for gold
description: It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground
body: It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and at least 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims."We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday."The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high – spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures."[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector."It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments"."As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects. Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common – whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear"."Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it."This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman."We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched."Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

schema.headline: Indonesia: 13 dead in mine disaster that highlights illegal hunt for gold

title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
description: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives
body: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend"."Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English."He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during WWII.Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.He said talks were expected to resume in December.On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.The Kremlin appears to be resisting.In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems."It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said."The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.So whose decision was that?"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.He declined to be more specific.But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.They have also plunged much of the city into darkness."[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said."People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

schema.headline: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough

title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
description: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approvedImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, SpaceX is an aerospace company that b
body: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approvedImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite servicesByMax MatzaUS regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind. The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth". "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said. Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use. Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them."That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet." Figure caption, The BBC visited Arizona before the US midterm elections to understand America's data-centre boomThe orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

schema.headline: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space

title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin ReuterByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News InvestigationsA German
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin ReuterByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News InvestigationsA German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police. Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled) At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.Image caption, One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cansThe case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show."Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boatsBoth men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.Image caption, Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German policeMeanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.Image caption, We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rulesWhen we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.Image caption, Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near DortmundIn Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds

title: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
description: Figure caption, Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's musicByMusic correspondentUpdated 26 November 2026Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod
body: Figure caption, Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's musicByMusic correspondentUpdated 26 November 2026Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music."His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart"."Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."Figure caption, Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order,  recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You. Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songsThe son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and new wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980sDuran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs. Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.They became so popular in the US that the press labeled them the leaders of a "second British invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station. The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid."We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy. "We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."He went on to play on Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.Image source, PAImage caption, Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse MacabreAfter a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again. In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion. When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.The following BBC programmes will pay tribute to Taylor: Duran Duran at the BBC, on BBC Four on Friday 27 November at 21:30 GMTSounds of the 80s, on Radio 2 on Saturday 28 November at at 18:00 GMT

schema.headline: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65

title: Muhoozi Kainerugaba: Ugandan president's son angers DR Congo with social media posts
description: The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainer
body: The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns. The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.The Ugandan government has yet to respond.The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours. Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province. They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo. "These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday. "The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future". The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

schema.headline: Muhoozi Kainerugaba: Ugandan president's son angers DR Congo with social media posts
